title: Behavioral Design Patterns: Strategy, Observer, Command, Iterator, State, Template Method, Chain of Responsibility
summary: Quick revision notes on seven behavioral design patterns: each one's intent, the mental model, when to use it, and how to tell look-alike patterns apart. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Behavioral Patterns: The Mental Model
points: Behavioral patterns govern how objects communicate and share responsibility; they move variation (an algorithm, a reaction, a request) out of the caller and behind an interface
One-line intent: Strategy = swap an algorithm; Observer = notify dependents of a change; Command = turn a request into an object; Iterator = traverse without exposing structure
One-line intent: State = behavior changes with internal state; Template Method = fixed skeleton, subclass fills steps; Chain of Responsibility = pass a request along handlers until one handles it
Mental shortcut: Template Method uses inheritance (compile-time, subclass); Strategy, State, Command, Observer, Chain use composition (runtime, swappable object)
Smell that signals a behavioral pattern: a long if/else or switch on type, flag or state that picks behavior, or a caller hard-wired to one concrete receiver

chapters.title: Strategy, State and Template Method
points: Strategy: client picks one interchangeable algorithm object (e.g. sort comparator, payment method, compression) behind one interface; context delegates to it and strategies never know each other
State: context holds a current state object and delegates; states themselves trigger transitions by replacing the context's state (e.g. TCP connection Open/Closed, Order Pending/Shipped)
Strategy vs State: identical class diagram; Strategy is chosen by the client and stays fixed, State changes itself automatically and states know about each other
Template Method: base class defines the algorithm skeleton as a final method calling abstract steps and optional hooks; subclasses override steps only (e.g. parse() = open, extract, close)

Template Method vs Strategy: inheritance varies parts of one algorithm at compile time; Strategy replaces the whole algorithm at runtime via composition; Template Method follows the Hollywood principle (the base class calls your steps, you don't call it); its trap is a rigid, deep inheritance hierarchy

chapters.title: Observer, Command and Mediator-Free Messaging
points: Observer: subject keeps a list of observers and calls notify() on change (subscribe/unsubscribe/notify); one-to-many, loosely coupled (e.g. DOM addEventListener, Redux subscribe)
Observer pitfalls: forgotten unsubscribe causes memory leaks (lapsed listener); notification order is not guaranteed; cascading updates can loop
Command: encapsulate a request as an object with execute() (and undo()) holding receiver and arguments; enables queues, logging, macros, undo/redo and retry (e.g. editor actions, job queue)
Command vs Strategy: Command is a request to be executed later by a receiver (has a receiver, often undoable); Strategy is how a context does one job and has no receiver
Observer vs Command: Observer broadcasts 'something happened' to many unknown listeners; Command is an explicit 'do this' addressed to one receiver, stored and replayable

chapters.title: Iterator and Chain of Responsibility
points: Iterator: provides sequential access (next/hasNext, or Python __iter__/__next__, JS Symbol.iterator, generators) to a collection without exposing its internal structure; supports multiple independent traversals
Iterator gotchas: modifying a collection while iterating raises ConcurrentModificationException in Java or skips items; an exhausted iterator cannot be reused
Chain of Responsibility: each handler either processes the request or passes it to the next handler (e.g. middleware, logging levels, support escalation); sender does not know which handler acts

Chain variants: classic stops at the first handler that handles it; middleware style lets every handler act then call next(); a request can fall off the end unhandled so add a default terminal handler
Chain vs Command: Chain routes one request to whichever handler can take it, Command packages a request for a known receiver; they combine well (commands passed through a handler chain)

chapters.title: Choosing the Right Pattern
points: Decision rule by question: need swappable algorithm -> Strategy; behavior depends on lifecycle status -> State; fixed steps with variable parts -> Template Method

Decision rule by question: many parties react to a change -> Observer; need undo, queue or log of actions -> Command; unknown handler picks up request -> Chain of Responsibility; hide traversal -> Iterator
Look-alike table: Strategy/State (who switches), Strategy/Template (composition vs inheritance), Command/Strategy (receiver and undo), Observer/Chain (all notified vs first handler wins)
Common mistakes: using State when two states exist and a boolean suffices; Strategy for an algorithm that never changes; Observer where a direct call is clearer; deep inheritance in Template Method
Trade-off: every pattern adds classes and indirection, so apply only when the variation is real (rule of thumb: the second or third variant)

chapters.title: Behavioral Patterns Cheat Sheet
points: Strategy: swap algorithm at runtime, client-chosen, composition; example: sort comparator
State: behavior follows internal state, object-driven transitions; example: order lifecycle
Template Method: skeleton in base class, steps in subclasses, inheritance; example: framework lifecycle hooks
Observer: one-to-many notify, unsubscribe to avoid leaks; example: event listeners
Command: request as object with execute/undo, queue and replay; example: editor undo stack
Iterator: traverse without exposing structure, one cursor per traversal; Chain: handlers pass along until one handles, add a default terminal handler
